input.raw_text: One inflation print and the market map has been redrawn. The cool CPI set off a rotation I have rarely seen in violence: small caps gapped and ran — the Russell up something like ten percent in days — while the mega-cap leaders are sold hard. For months the story was concentration, AI winners, fewer stocks carrying the market, and suddenly the laggards are the trade and everyone forced into megacaps for liquidity is reversing. Whether it lasts is the debate on every call I take. The bull case: an easing cycle flatters small caps with their floating-rate debt and cyclical exposure. The bear case: one print does not make a trend, and the squeeze includes fast money chasing underperformance that leaves as fast as it came. The megacap selloff is orderly — reallocation, not de-risking. If small caps hold for two more weeks, the regime has genuinely changed.
input.summary: A cooler inflation reading triggered an unusually sharp rotation from previously dominant mega-cap leaders toward small-cap laggards, with the Russell rising approximately ten percent within days. The mega-cap decline appears orderly and consistent with reallocation rather than broad risk reduction. The durability of the shift remains uncertain because it follows a single inflation release and may partly reflect short-lived performance chasing, while prospective monetary easing could provide more persistent support for rate-sensitive and cyclical small companies.

Approximate ten-percent Russell advance within days
Abrupt reversal of prolonged market concentration
Orderly mega-cap selling consistent with reallocation
Potential small-cap support from easing and cyclical sensitivity
Possible short-lived performance chasing after prolonged underperformance
Durability uncertain after a single inflation release
Two-week persistence identified as evidence of a lasting regime shift
